paragraphs: Observational data can make a treatment appear to cause an outcome when an unseen variable actually influences both. This paper studies that problem when many treatments share hidden confounding. Its central question is when those shared patterns contain enough information to identify the effects of interventions, despite the confounder remaining unobserved.

The key idea is to use some treatments as proxies for the hidden confounder when studying interventions on the remaining treatments. Those proxy treatments provide indirect information about the common source of bias. The paper develops conditions under which this perspective permits causal identification; the presence of many treatments alone is not presented as sufficient.

The authors also show how directly modeling the observed data can avoid solving the integral equations used in existing proxy-variable identification formulas. They extend their results to a broader class of causal graphs containing additional confounders and selection variables. Together, these contributions connect shared confounding to proxy-based identification and offer a different route for obtaining intervention distributions.
icml-2021-a-proxy-variable-view-of-share.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for identifying causal effects by using some treatments as proxies for confounders shared with other treatments.

paragraphs: Reducing a convolutional network's computation often means shrinking its depth, width, or input resolution. The paper argues that concentrating all pruning on one dimension can shrink it excessively and cause a large accuracy loss. It proposes choosing reductions across all three dimensions together to meet a computational budget more effectively.

The framework learns a polynomial relationship between model accuracy and the three dimensions. It then optimizes that polynomial to select depth, width, and resolution values and prunes the network accordingly. The selected configuration is therefore guided by an estimated accuracy relationship, with the three choices considered jointly rather than independently.

Collecting enough measurements to fit that relationship can itself be expensive. The authors address this by specializing the polynomial to work with less training data and using repeated pruning and fine-tuning to gather data faster. Their experiments report better results than leading pruning methods and even architecture-search approaches. The findings support coordinated pruning as a useful way to allocate reductions across a network.
icml-2021-accelerate-cnns-from-three-dim.tldr: This pruning framework jointly selects network depth, width, and resolution using a learned polynomial model of accuracy.

paragraphs: Collecting only part of a signal can reduce acquisition time, data transfer, battery use, or radiation exposure, depending on the application. Deep Probabilistic Subsampling integrates the choice of measurements into a model trained from input to output. Its restriction is that the learned sampling pattern stays the same for every data point.

Active-DPS changes this into a sequential process. After obtaining some measurements, the method uses the information already collected to choose the next sample. This lets acquisition respond to the particular signal being examined. The contribution is an adaptive extension of the existing learned subsampling approach, linking successive measurement choices to what the model has observed.

The authors report improvements over the static method on MNIST classification at high subsampling rates. They also demonstrate strong results for actively acquiring measurements for MRI reconstruction, outperforming DPS and other deep learning methods in their evaluation. These findings support adapting acquisition to each example when only a subset of the signal is collected.
icml-2021-active-deep-probabilistic-subs.tldr: Active-DPS chooses each new measurement using previously acquired information, improving reported classification and MRI reconstruction results over static subsampling.

paragraphs: Weight-sharing architecture search trains many candidate networks inside one larger supernet. The smaller networks learn partly by matching the supernet's predictions, making knowledge distillation important to their performance. This paper identifies a potential problem with the commonly used KL divergence: students may learn predictions that misrepresent the teacher's uncertainty in either direction.

The proposed training approach uses the more general alpha-divergence and chooses it adaptively. The authors describe this adaptation as preventing both overestimation and underestimation of teacher uncertainty. This makes the way knowledge is transferred a central design choice, rather than treating the standard distillation objective as fixed.

The approach improves both slimmable networks and weight-sharing architecture search in the reported experiments. The resulting AlphaNet model family outperforms BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS across a range of computation budgets. One reported model reaches 80.0% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at 444 million FLOPs. The results show that changing supernet training can improve the smaller architectures obtained from it.
icml-2021-alphanet-improved-training-of-.tldr: AlphaNet improves supernet training through adaptive alpha-divergence distillation that better preserves teacher uncertainty in smaller networks.

paragraphs: A few examples rarely determine a concept uniquely. A scene might qualify because of its objects' colors, their shapes, their number, or a combination of those properties. CURI turns this ambiguity into a benchmark for learning compositional concepts, asking models to reason when several explanations remain compatible with limited observations.

The benchmark consists of few-shot meta-learning tasks in a concept space that supports constructing new concepts from components. Its evaluation splits test different forms of systematic generalization, including separating factors, combining concepts productively, learning Boolean operations, and binding variables. This makes uncertainty part of concept acquisition itself, rather than evaluating composition only after the relevant rule is established.

The authors also introduce a model-independent compositionality gap for comparing how difficult the different out-of-distribution splits are. That measure helps distinguish the challenge posed by a split from the performance of a particular model. Evaluations across multiple modeling choices reveal substantial remaining room for improvement, positioning CURI as a test of compositional learning under genuinely ambiguous evidence.
icml-2021-curi-a-benchmark-for-productiv.tldr: CURI tests whether models can learn and recombine concepts from few examples while accounting for uncertainty about the underlying rule.

paragraphs: Training decision trees to resist adversarial examples can be computationally expensive. The paper introduces GROOT, an algorithm for robust decision trees and random forests, to reduce that expense. It reports training times of seconds to minutes where existing leading approaches require hours, making training speed a central contribution.

The main technical change concerns the worst-case Gini impurity calculation used during robust training. Earlier methods compute this quantity iteratively. The authors derive an analytical solution, reducing the calculation's complexity from linear in the number of samples to constant time. This claim applies to that computation, rather than implying that an entire tree can be trained in constant time.

The evaluation covers individual trees and ensembles on 14 structured datasets, alongside MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. GROOT runs several orders of magnitude faster than the compared leading methods and achieves better adversarial accuracy on structured data. The stated results therefore combine a substantial efficiency improvement with improved robustness performance in the structured-data evaluations.
icml-2021-efficient-training-of-robust-d.tldr: GROOT accelerates robust tree training with an analytical impurity calculation and reports better adversarial accuracy on structured data.

paragraphs: Graph representation methods can require extensive expert effort to tune their hyperparameters. Automating that search can reduce the burden, but a search procedure may still provide little explanation of which settings matter. This paper develops e-AutoGR to automate graph representation learning while exposing the relative importance of different hyperparameters.

The method uses explainable graph features when estimating model performance. It then learns importance weights through a nonlinear regression procedure designed to decorrelate the weighting of hyperparameters. These weights provide information about how different hyperparameters affect performance and can inform interpretation of the search process. The explanation concerns the tuning choices behind a representation model.

The authors provide a theoretical argument for the soundness of the decorrelated weighting algorithm. Experiments on real-world datasets report improvements over leading methods in both model performance and the explainability of hyperparameter importance. The contribution therefore joins automated tuning with a structured account of which choices influence its results, rather than treating search quality as the only objective.
icml-2021-explainable-automated-graph-re.tldr: e-AutoGR automates graph representation tuning while learning interpretable importance weights for the hyperparameters that affect performance.

paragraphs: Recommendation algorithms determine which items receive attention and, consequently, which sellers, artists, or writers benefit from being seen. The paper argues that a conventional bandit objective can concentrate exposure on a winner in an undesirable way. It introduces an objective that incorporates merit-based fairness to items while still optimizing user utility.

The authors formalize two forms of regret: one tracks fairness and the other tracks reward. Keeping both quantities explicit makes it possible to study whether an algorithm learns to provide useful recommendations while also allocating exposure appropriately. They develop algorithms for stochastic multi-armed bandits and stochastic linear bandits within this setting.

The theoretical results establish sublinear growth of both fairness regret and reward regret. This means that each cumulative shortfall grows more slowly than the number of decisions, so its average per decision diminishes. Empirical results also support effective exposure allocation across arms. The fairness claim is tied to the paper's merit-based objective, which makes item exposure a direct part of learning.
icml-2021-fairness-of-exposure-in-stocha.tldr: The paper introduces bandit algorithms that balance user reward with merit-based item exposure and achieve sublinear regret for both objectives.

paragraphs: Stackelberg prediction games model interactions between a learner and a data provider during training. These problems are often difficult bilevel optimizations, but a special class using least-squares loss admits a polynomial-time solution. The existing approach nevertheless requires solving a semidefinite program at every step of a bisection procedure, creating substantial computational overhead.

This paper reformulates the least-squares game as a single semidefinite program. Its form and dimension are similar to the programs repeatedly solved by the earlier method, but the reformulation removes the repeated sequence of solves. The authors then show that this program can be reduced further to a second-order cone program.

Experiments find the single-semidefinite-program formulation orders of magnitude faster than bisection. The second-order cone formulation produces reported speedups of up to more than 20,000 times over the state of the art on synthetic and real-world datasets, supporting real-time responses for large problems. These improvements apply to the least-squares subclass studied, rather than resolving the general difficulty of Stackelberg prediction games.
icml-2021-fast-algorithms-for-stackelber.tldr: New optimization reformulations greatly accelerate least-squares Stackelberg prediction games, with reported speedups exceeding 20,000 times in some experiments.

paragraphs: When a multi-agent system contains very many agents, a mean-field problem can provide an approximation of its behavior. This paper studies policy-gradient methods for both mean-field control and mean-field games. It focuses on continuous-time models, extending a research direction in which much recent policy-gradient work had used discrete time.

The analysis assumes that agents have identical linear state transitions and quadratic cost functions. Within this structured setting, the authors provide policy-gradient updates for both problems and establish convergence to the optimal solution at a linear rate. Here, linear convergence describes a geometric reduction in optimization error as updates proceed, rather than a claim about how runtime scales with the number of agents.

A synthetic simulation verifies the reported convergence behavior. For the game formulation, the paper also gives sufficient conditions for a Nash equilibrium to exist and be unique. Those conditions establish one route to existence and uniqueness; they are not claimed to be necessary. The contribution is a convergence analysis for policy-gradient learning in these continuous-time, linear-quadratic mean-field settings.
icml-2021-global-convergence-of-policy-g.tldr: The paper proves linear-rate policy-gradient convergence for continuous-time linear-quadratic mean-field control and games under its stated modeling assumptions.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning represents how strongly different labels describe an example, yet it is often used for classification. This paper identifies a mismatch between learning that distribution and achieving the classification objective. A method can therefore optimize its distribution-learning goal without being as well aligned with selecting the appropriate class as intended.

The proposed Label Distribution Learning Machine addresses the mismatch by extending margin theory to this setting. The authors define a label distribution margin and introduce a Support Vector Regression Machine to learn the optimal label. They also develop an adaptive margin loss for learning label description degrees, connecting these degrees to the broader classification-oriented approach.

The paper develops a generalization theory for the regression component and analyzes generalization for the complete method. Experiments report better classification performance for LDLM. The significance is the explicit treatment of objective alignment: when a distribution-learning method is used to classify, its training formulation should account for the classification goal as well as the label description degrees.
icml-2021-label-distribution-learning-ma.tldr: LDLM uses margin-based learning to better align label distribution learning with classification and reports improved classification performance.

paragraphs: Average-reward Markov decision processes focus on the reward achieved over ongoing interaction. This paper introduces learning and planning algorithms for that setting, including off-policy methods, which learn about a policy using experience that can come from another policy. A central aim is to provide convergence guarantees without awkward dependence on designated reference states.

The shared algorithmic change is to update the average-reward estimate using temporal-difference error instead of the conventional error. The authors establish a general convergent off-policy model-free control algorithm without reference states and a convergent off-policy model-free prediction algorithm. They also introduce an off-policy algorithm that reaches the actual value function rather than a version shifted by an offset.

These are presented as first results of their respective kinds. Experiments on an access-control queuing task illustrate difficulties that reference-state methods can encounter, and the authors argue that their alternatives are significantly easier to use. The paper thus connects a change in the reward-estimation update to both convergence results and a reduction in practical setup difficulties.
icml-2021-learning-and-planning-in-avera.tldr: Temporal-difference updates enable new proven-convergent off-policy algorithms for average-reward learning, including control without reference states.

paragraphs: A learned controller can perform well on familiar tasks yet struggle when their structure changes. This paper investigates whether part of that difficulty comes from handling new combinations of familiar elements. It offers evidence that combinatorial generalization is often a bottleneck, helping explain why standard architectures may need extensive data to generalize.

For a particular subclass of Markov decision processes, the authors embed a time-dependent shortest-path solver inside a deep neural network policy. The architecture therefore includes an explicit algorithmic component for the relevant structured problem. It is trained end to end through blackbox differentiation, allowing the solver-containing policy to participate in the learning process.

The reported result is a considerable improvement in generalization when training data are limited. The scope matters: the approach is demonstrated for the stated subclass of decision problems, rather than claimed to solve generalization across all control tasks. Its main implication is that supplying a suitable algorithmic structure can alleviate a combinatorial obstacle that additional training data would otherwise have to address.
icml-2021-neuro-algorithmic-policies-ena.tldr: Embedding a shortest-path solver in a learned policy improves low-data generalization for a particular subclass of decision problems.

paragraphs: Recognizing an image and locating its foreground object place different demands on a model. Object segmentation requires separating relevant pixels from the background, which makes it a more detailed task than image classification. This paper asks whether large-scale unsupervised models can support that separation without either image-level labels or pixel-level annotations.

The authors show that recent unsupervised generative adversarial networks contain information that can distinguish foreground pixels from background pixels. They use this capability to produce high-quality saliency masks. These masks identify the foreground region, making the learned information useful for segmentation rather than only for whole-image representations or classification.

Extensive comparisons on common benchmarks show better performance than existing unsupervised object-segmentation alternatives, establishing a new state of the art in the reported evaluation. The finding extends the usefulness of unsupervised generative models to a task requiring spatially detailed output. Its significance is that the demonstrated segmentation process does not depend on human labeling at either the image or pixel level.
icml-2021-object-segmentation-without-la.tldr: Large-scale unsupervised GANs can produce foreground segmentation masks without image or pixel labels, outperforming evaluated unsupervised alternatives.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning represents data using combinations of a small set of basic elements. Applying that idea to graphs is difficult because graphs can occupy different metric spaces, lack corresponding nodes, and contain different numbers of nodes. This paper proposes an online dictionary-learning method that accommodates those differences through a graph-specific fitting objective.

Each graph is described by pairwise relations between its nodes and modeled as a convex combination of graph atoms, the learned dictionary elements. The fitting term uses Gromov Wasserstein divergence. An online stochastic algorithm learns the atoms from unregistered graphs, including datasets whose graphs vary in size, and the approach also extends to labeled graphs.

The authors additionally derive an upper bound that provides a fast approximation of Gromov Wasserstein in the embedding space. Numerical results support the method's usefulness for unsupervised graph embeddings and for estimating and tracking graph subspaces online. The contribution makes dictionary-style representations available for graph collections where direct correspondence between the original objects is absent.
icml-2021-online-graph-dictionary-learni.tldr: The method learns graph dictionaries online using Gromov Wasserstein fitting, accommodating graphs with unmatched nodes and different sizes.

paragraphs: A cardinality constraint limits how many variables in an optimization solution can be nonzero. This paper studies convex quadratic objectives with that additional sparsity requirement. It builds a hierarchy of approximations using the dominant eigenvectors of the quadratic matrix, so the matrix's leading directions guide how the optimization problem is simplified.

Each approximation has a min-max formulation with a useful separation between discrete and continuous choices. The binary variables can be optimized analytically while the problem retains convexity in its continuous variables. The authors use this property to develop two scalable algorithms, called best response and dual program, for screening candidate locations of nonzero entries.

Screening helps narrow the indices that need attention in the original sparse problem. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the proposed methods are competitive with existing screening approaches in sparse regression. They are particularly fast on instances with many measurements. The contribution is therefore an approximation-based route to efficient screening, supported by favorable results in that high-measurement setting.
icml-2021-principal-component-hierarchy-.tldr: A principal-component approximation hierarchy enables scalable screening for sparse quadratic optimization, with particularly fast reported results on high-measurement problems.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy that becomes safe after training may still violate constraints while learning. This paper addresses safety during exploration in an unknown Markov decision process, focusing on chance constraints, which express safety requirements probabilistically. The goal is to learn a rewarding policy while respecting those requirements throughout the learning process.

SAILR uses an intervention mechanism based on advantage functions to protect the agent during training. Alongside that mechanism, it optimizes the policy with existing reinforcement-learning algorithms designed for unconstrained problems. The method comes with guarantees covering training safety, deployment safety without the intervention mechanism, and performance relative to the optimal safety-constrained policy.

In experiments, SAILR incurs far fewer training-time constraint violations than standard safe reinforcement-learning and constrained-MDP approaches. It also converges to a well-performing policy that can operate safely without intervention. The result links protected exploration to independent deployment: intervention supports learning, while the eventual policy is intended to satisfy the chance-constrained safety objective after that support is removed.
icml-2021-safe-reinforcement-learning-us.tldr: SAILR uses advantage-based interventions to support safe training and learns policies with safety guarantees for deployment without intervention.

paragraphs: Learning from few labels creates difficulties for both semi-supervised learning and transfer learning. Self-training from scratch can be misled by incorrect pseudo-labels, especially when many classes are possible. Fine-tuning a pretrained model on limited labeled data can also transfer poorly when it does not exploit the structure in available unlabeled examples.

Self-Tuning combines these two sources of help: transferring a pretrained model and learning from both labeled and unlabeled target data. It also introduces Pseudo Group Contrast, a mechanism designed to reduce dependence on pseudo-labels and increase tolerance to incorrect ones. The approach tackles unreliable inferred labels while bringing unlabeled-data structure into the transfer process.

The reported evaluation finds substantial improvements over semi-supervised and transfer-learning counterparts across five tasks. On Cars with 15% of the labels available, Self-Tuning doubles the accuracy of fine-tuning. This result illustrates the potential value of combining pretraining with unlabeled-data learning, while the broader contribution is a unified training approach designed to address weaknesses of either strategy used alone.
icml-2021-self-tuning-for-data-efficient.tldr: Self-Tuning combines pretrained-model transfer with labeled and unlabeled data, using Pseudo Group Contrast to tolerate inaccurate pseudo-labels.

paragraphs: Making a pretrained network's weights sparse is useful when deployment memory is limited. This paper gives a new mathematical formulation of that task. Instead of treating sparsity only as a direct search over weights to remove, it uses properties of the network's activation functions to express the problem in another optimization form.

The authors show an equivalence to an approximate subdifferential inclusion problem, with the accuracy of the approximation controlling sparsity. The formulation applies to a broad class of activation functions, including ReLU, sigmoid, and softmax. This makes the activation's mathematical structure part of the sparsification method and provides an explicit connection between approximation and sparse weights.

They propose an iterative optimization algorithm with a convergence guarantee. Its flexibility also allows sparsity to be induced using partial training data in minibatches. Experiments cover image classification, speech recognition, natural language processing, and time-series forecasting. These evaluations demonstrate the approach across several application contexts, while the central contribution is a convergent optimization framework for sparsifying existing networks.
icml-2021-sparsifying-networks-via-subdi.tldr: The paper reformulates pretrained-network sparsification as approximate subdifferential inclusion and develops a convergent minibatch-compatible algorithm.

paragraphs: Exploration can collect information about an environment without prioritizing what matters for the eventual task. This paper asks precisely what an agent needs to learn for a particular decision problem. It studies a broad class of tasks in linear dynamical systems, including the linear quadratic regulator problem.

The authors derive lower bounds that depend on both the particular system and the task, quantifying the difficulty of gathering enough information. Those bounds motivate an efficient exploration algorithm based on experiment design. Finite-time guarantees show that its sample requirements match the instance- and task-dependent optimum up to constant factors within the studied setting.

Examples involving linear quadratic regulators establish provable improvements over exploration that ignores the task. The paper also proves instance- and task-optimality for certainty-equivalence decision making and presents the first instance-optimal algorithm for the regulator problem. Experiments illustrate practical effectiveness. Together, the results make task relevance a precise criterion for exploration, connecting what the agent measures to the decision it ultimately needs to make.
icml-2021-task-optimal-exploration-in-li.tldr: Task-guided experiment design achieves instance- and task-optimal exploration sample complexity up to constant factors for the studied linear-system problems.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization searches for good choices when the objective must be evaluated rather than optimized through an available explicit formula. Bayesian optimization has succeeded on continuous domains, but high-dimensional categorical spaces remain challenging. The difficulty also extends to mixed spaces, where some choices are categories and others are continuous values.

The paper proposes combining local optimization with a kernel designed for these search spaces. The kernel supplies the modeling structure used by the optimization approach, while local search is part of how it handles many dimensions. The authors report that this combination retains sample efficiency, addressing the number of objective evaluations as well as the structure of the search.

The work includes a convergence guarantee and experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks. The reported method outperforms existing baselines in solution performance, computational cost, or both, depending on the comparison. These findings support the combination of local optimization and tailored modeling for categorical and mixed domains, without claiming simultaneous improvement on every measure in every task.
icml-2021-think-global-and-act-local-bay.tldr: A tailored kernel combined with local optimization improves Bayesian optimization in high-dimensional categorical and mixed search spaces.

paragraphs: Contrastive self-supervised learning often depends on domain-specific transformations that create useful related examples. Image cropping and rotation are examples of choices that require knowledge of the data. DACL addresses situations where such transformations are not readily available, seeking a way to construct contrastive training examples across different kinds of data.

Its central ingredient is Mixup noise: samples are mixed differently to create similar and dissimilar examples. Mixing can take place at the input level or within a model's hidden representations. This gives the contrastive learning process a source of variation that does not depend on designing a separate augmentation procedure for each domain.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing advantages over Gaussian-noise-based contrastive learning. Experiments span tabular data, images, and graphs, with DACL outperforming other domain-agnostic noising approaches in the reported results. It also combines with domain-specific methods such as SimCLR to improve visual representations. The findings support both its use where tailored augmentations are unavailable and its compatibility with existing image-specific approaches.
icml-2021-towards-domain-agnostic-contra.tldr: DACL uses sample mixing for contrastive learning across domains and can also improve representations when combined with domain-specific augmentations.

paragraphs: Some learning problems optimize parameters through a sequence of computations, as in recurrent networks, learned optimizers, or hyperparameter tuning through training steps. Estimating gradients through these unrolled graphs can involve high memory use, slow updates, high variance, or bias. This paper proposes Persistent Evolution Strategies to improve that combination of tradeoffs.

PES divides the computation into shorter unrolls and performs an evolution-strategies update after each segment. Simply truncating a sequence can introduce bias. PES addresses that problem by accumulating correction terms across the entire sequence of unrolls, preserving information needed to eliminate the bias caused by those truncations.

The resulting estimator is described as unbiased, memory efficient, and capable of rapid parameter updates, with reasonable variance characteristics. Synthetic-task experiments demonstrate advantages over several other gradient-estimation methods. Further experiments show applicability to learned-optimizer training and hyperparameter tuning. The contribution is a way to update frequently from short computation segments while maintaining correction terms that account for the longer sequence.
icml-2021-unbiased-gradient-estimation-i.tldr: PES accumulates correction terms across truncated unrolls to obtain unbiased gradient estimates with low memory use and frequent updates.

paragraphs: Preprocessing and optimization choices can affect which information a model uses to generalize. This paper shows that data whitening and certain second-order optimization schemes can reduce or even prevent generalization. Its explanation centers on the sample-sample second moment matrix, which captures relationships among examples that training can exploit.

For the studied class of models with a fully connected first layer, the authors prove that this matrix contains the only information available for generalization under their theoretical setup. Whitening or certain second-order updates reduce access to that information. The resulting loss of usable structure explains why better-conditioned training need not lead to better performance on new examples.

Experiments on several architectures verify the predictions and show that generalization can still suffer when the theoretical requirements are relaxed. However, regularized second-order optimization provides an empirical tradeoff: it can accelerate training while discarding less information, and sometimes even improve generalization. The findings therefore distinguish harmful information loss from cases where regularization preserves a useful balance between optimization speed and predictive performance.
icml-2021-whitening-and-second-order-opt.tldr: Whitening and certain second-order updates can remove usable generalization information, while regularization can provide a better speed–generalization tradeoff.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a compact student to imitate a larger teacher, commonly using the teacher's softmax outputs. This paper studies a more restricted setting: the teacher's parameters are inaccessible, and it returns only predicted classes. The challenge is to recover useful training guidance from those decisions without access to the teacher's probability outputs.

When training examples are available, the method computes their distances to the teacher's decision boundaries. Those distances represent how robust an example is against assignment to other classes and are used to construct soft labels. The student can then be trained with standard distillation using these reconstructed targets.

The authors also handle the case where the original training data are unavailable. They generate pseudo examples designed to be distinguished as much as possible by the teacher's decision boundaries, then construct soft labels to form a transfer set. Evaluations across benchmark networks and datasets demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution is a boundary-based route to distillation under both restricted teacher access and, in the extended setting, missing training data.
icml-2021-zero-shot-knowledge-distillati.tldr: The method distills class-only black-box teachers by constructing soft labels from decision boundaries, including when original training data are unavailable.
